# Scope


<!-- WARNING: THIS FILE WAS AUTOGENERATED! DO NOT EDIT! -->

edgeslm fine-tunes small language models (SLMs) for narrow tasks and
runs them on edge hardware. This page describes the approach through its
first task: short WhatsApp messages that tell coffee farmers which
plants are short of water and which sensors need fixing. It is a working
document, and its sections change as we refine the approach.

## Problem and framing

A large hosted model can already do an expert’s analysis. In the [batch
2
diagnosis](https://fr.anckalbi.net/speaking-plants/batches/b02/diagnosis.html)
of speaking-plants, Claude found the water-stressed plant from the
sensor logs, much as a plant physiologist would. Using such a model for
every message in the field has costs:

- every call costs money and energy,
- farm data leaves the farm,
- the service depends on a provider, and on the network at the moment of
  the call,
- a narrow, repeated task uses only a small part of the model’s
  expertise.

edgeslm takes the other route: a small model, fine-tuned for one narrow
task, that runs on a board on the farm. The model is like a chip that
holds one slice of domain expertise. The pipeline that builds it is
domain-neutral: a task is defined by data, namely its input format, its
output format and its examples.

### The first task

The first task comes from
[speaking-plants](https://fr.anckalbi.net/speaking-plants/), which
detects water stress in coffee plants with thermal cameras, soil
moisture sensors and an air sensor. Sensors are costly to run, so only
some plants carry a sensor node: a farm can have dozens of nodes, each
standing for the plants around it. The task has two parts:

- **Triage, in code.** Feature engineering and a classical ML model
  decide, for one farm and one day, which nodes to watch or fix, how
  severe each case is, and what the data shows about its cause, such as
  whether water still reaches the soil. This part belongs to the domain
  project, not to edgeslm.
- **The message, by the SLM.** The model turns the triage into a short
  WhatsApp message to the farmer.

Deciding what is critical is the code’s job. Saying it clearly, with an
action, is the model’s job.

The message follows these rules:

- It covers only the nodes to watch or fix. When nothing is critical,
  nothing is sent.
- It says what to do, such as watering or maintenance. It gives no
  measurements or counts: a value such as a leaf-to-air temperature
  difference means little to a farmer as an absolute number, and the
  engineered features and the ML model already capture the signal. A
  count of flagged nodes would mislead too, because only some plants are
  monitored and a problem on a shared line usually reaches the plants
  between them.
- It covers two kinds of problem: water stress, and equipment faults
  such as a failed sensor or a silent node.
- Each item is one paragraph: its severity marker, its location exactly
  as in the triage, a colon, then what is wrong and what to do. The
  markers are 👀 early, ⚠️ moderate and 🚨 severe. Later mentions use
  words such as “the line” or “its dripper”, not the location again.
- Its paragraphs follow the triage’s order, most severe first, and say
  when each problem started with the triage’s phrase, such as since
  today, since Tuesday or for a week or more. It never gives a date.
- It is at most 600 characters long, so that it fits on a phone screen.
- It is sent in the evening or early in the morning, before irrigation.
  Water stress shows most clearly in the afternoon.

Here is a sketch of one triage output and its message, for an invented
farm with 40 sensor nodes. The triage contract, below, defines its
fields and rules:

``` json
{
  "farm": "fazenda-exemplo", "date": "2026-10-08", "nodes": 40,
  "items": [
    {"problem": "water stress", "location": "Block B, drip line B2", "pattern": "cluster",
     "nodes_flagged": 6, "nodes_in_group": 8, "severity": "moderate", "since": "since Tuesday",
     "soil_water": "none since Tuesday"},
    {"problem": "equipment fault", "location": "Block A, row 1", "pattern": "one node",
     "severity": "moderate", "since": "since Monday", "fault": "missing data"},
    {"problem": "water stress", "location": "Block C, row 3", "pattern": "one node",
     "severity": "early", "since": "since today", "soil_water": "arriving"}
  ]
}
```

> ⚠️ Block B, drip line B2: most monitored plants have been short of
> water since Tuesday, and no water has reached their soil since then.
> Check the line today, from its start to the last plant.
>
> ⚠️ Block A, row 1: the sensors at this plant have sent no data since
> Monday, so it is not monitored. Check the node’s power and connection.
>
> 👀 Block C, row 3: a monitored plant has shown first signs of water
> stress since today, although its soil still gets water. Check the
> plant for heat damage or root problems.

### Language

The farmers in the first task read Brazilian Portuguese. Small models
are usually weaker in Portuguese than in English, so the baseline
measures candidate models in Portuguese before any fine-tuning.
Fine-tuning should help: it picks up style and vocabulary from little
data, and regional farm vocabulary is that kind of target. If small
models still fall short, a fixed template can carry the locations,
markers and actions, and the model writes only the rest. The proof of
concept uses English.

### Hardware

The model runs with llama.cpp on the gateway, the board that collects
the nodes’ data over LoRa radio. Two boards are candidates. [Rovai
compared both](https://mjrovai.com/articles/slm-edge-boards-compared/)
with the same models and the same llama.cpp build:

</tr>

The UNO Q comes in a 2 GB and a 4 GB version. The [4 GB
version](https://store.arduino.cc/products/uno-q-4gb) (ABX00173) has 4
GB of LPDDR4 memory and 32 GB of eMMC storage, and costs €82.90 with VAT
on the Arduino store in November 2026. The memory estimates in this
section are for the 4 GB version.

Messages are generated once a day per farm, so speed is not the main
limit. On the UNO Q, Qwen3.5 2B generated 2.53 tokens per second, so a
message of about 100 tokens takes under a minute. Memory sets the limit
instead: by our estimate, about 4B parameters on the Pi 5 and about 2B
on the UNO Q. The choice of board follows from the evaluation: the
smallest model that meets the quality threshold decides the cheapest
board that can run it. The fine-tuned Qwen3.5 0.8B passes every check in
264 of the 270 test messages and fits in the UNO Q’s memory, so the UNO
Q is the target board.

The fine-tuned model needs only the triage record and a one-line
instruction, with no rules or examples. On the UNO Q, the A53 cores must
process the whole prompt before they write the message. By our estimate,
the untuned models’ prompt of about 1,300 tokens would take longer to
process than the message takes to write. The run on the board will
measure this.

Sending a WhatsApp message needs a network connection, so a hosted model
would often be reachable too. The case for a local model rests on the
other reasons: data stays on the farm, there is no cost per message,
energy use is low, nothing depends on a provider, and generation does
not wait for the network, because the gateway can queue the message
until the connection is back.

## Pipeline

Building a model for a task follows these stages:

1.  **Synthetic triage inputs**, sampled across the task’s dimensions,
    as the next section describes.
2.  **Teacher messages:** a large model, Claude, writes the message for
    each input.
3.  **Baseline:** candidate base models write messages for the test
    inputs before any fine-tuning.
4.  **Fine-tuning:** LoRA adapters trained on pairs of inputs and
    messages. On Apple Silicon this uses MLX; on CUDA GPUs, tools such
    as unsloth do the same job. The fine-tuned model is prompted with
    the triage record and a one-line instruction: it learns the rules
    and the format from the examples.
5.  **Evaluation** of the baseline and fine-tuned models on the same
    held-out test set.
6.  **Export:** the adapter is fused into the base model and converted
    to GGUF, the single-file format that llama.cpp loads.
7.  **Deployment** on the target board with llama.cpp, and a final
    evaluation there.

Domain experts improve the data at stages 1, 2 and 5.

Over time, the two kinds of model take different roles. A large model is
the teacher during development, and handles new kinds of cases when a
connection is available. The small model handles the repeated task in
the field.

### Choice of teacher

Claude Haiku writes the teacher messages. Sonnet’s judgement of actions
and urgency looked somewhat better on a first batch of ten inputs, at
about three times the cost, so the first training set has a message from
each model for each of its 200 inputs. The two models wrote the same
message, word for word, for 73 of the 200 inputs, and their messages are
92% similar on average: the rules and examples leave little room for a
model’s own judgement. A comparison of the two teachers would measure
almost nothing, so the cheaper one, Haiku, is the teacher from now on,
and the student trains on its messages.

Each message records the model that wrote it, the temperature, the
version of the prompt and the date, so that messages written with
different prompts are never compared.

## Synthetic data generation

Synthetic inputs follow the method of [synthetic questions for
MARIS](https://fr.anckalbi.net/posts/synthetic-questions-maris/): find
the dimensions along which cases vary, give each a few levels, and
sample combinations of levels, called tuples. Each tuple stands for a
distinct case the model must handle. A few dimensions keep every tuple
covered. Ten dimensions with a few levels each would give tens of
thousands of tuples, most of them never sampled.

The first task has three dimensions with three levels each, so 27
tuples:

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Dimension</th>
<th>Levels</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Problem</td>
<td>water stress, equipment fault, both</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Spatial pattern</td>
<td>one node, a cluster sharing a line or block, widespread</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Severity</td>
<td>early, moderate, severe</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

The levels mean different things for the two kinds of problem:

- **Spatial pattern.** For water stress, one node points to a single
  plant or dripper, a cluster to a shared irrigation line, and
  widespread stress to the weather or the irrigation schedule.
  `soil_water` tells these apart: when water still arrives, the weather
  is the likelier cause. For equipment faults, one node points to that
  node, a cluster to what its nodes share, such as their power supply,
  and widespread faults to the gateway.
- **Severity.** For water stress, it is the plant’s state: first signs
  (early), stress for several days (moderate), or a risk of damage
  (severe). For equipment faults, it is how long and how badly data is
  lost, whatever the spatial pattern: data missing for hours,
  implausible values or a changed camera view (early), no data for 1 to
  3 days (moderate), or no data for more than 3 days (severe).

A node that sends no readings cannot be flagged for water stress, as the
triage contract below requires, because there is no data to detect
stress from. So when a `both` record has a widespread pattern and a
moderate or severe severity, the widespread item is the water stress,
and the fault is a single node or a cluster. With this rule all 27
tuples are valid, and a widespread, severe fault is a farm left
unmonitored for days.

Other variation changes the details of a message but not its kind, so it
is drawn at random within each tuple rather than made a dimension: farm
size, how locations are named (blocks and rows, numbered plots,
greenhouse benches), how long the problem has lasted, and the number of
items.

The test set has 10 inputs per tuple, 270 in total, and no test input is
ever used for training. Training sets are sampled across all tuples, so
scores can be broken down by tuple to show which cases a model gets
wrong.

## Triage contract

The proof of concept replaces the domain project’s triage with generated
records, from [`01_coffee`](../01_coffee.ipynb). The generator is a
mock, but every rule it follows to keep records consistent is also a
requirement on the real triage. This section lists the fields and rules,
so that the domain project and edgeslm agree on what the triage
delivers. The generator is the executable form of this contract: its
tests check every rule on every record of the test set.

### Rules

- **Readable locations.** Locations are names the farmer uses, such as a
  block and drip line, a row, a plot or a bench. They are never node
  IDs.
- **Groups follow irrigation.** A cluster is a group of nodes on one
  irrigation line or valve, so that its action, such as checking the
  line, reaches all the plants it covers.
- **One location, one item.** No two items point at the same node or
  group.
- **Most severe first.** Items are sorted by severity, most severe
  first, so that the message can keep their order.
- **Aggregation.** When one kind of problem flags more than 70% of the
  farm’s nodes, the triage reports one widespread item with one cause,
  not several local ones. The single nodes and clusters of one kind stay
  below that threshold.
- **No stress without data.** A node that sends no readings is reported
  as a fault, and is never flagged for water stress.
- **Observed causes.** A water stress item says through `soil_water`
  whether water reaches the soil, which the soil sensors show directly
  as a rise after irrigation or rain. The message gives the action at
  the level the data supports, such as checking the line, and never
  names a part that no sensor watches, such as a valve. An equipment
  fault item says through `fault` what the data shows, and `sensor`
  names the sensor when values are implausible. Its action says where to
  look, by pattern: one node, that node; several nodes, what they share,
  such as the gateway or the power supply.
- **No raw values.** Weather, readings and engineered features stay
  inside the ML model. They reach the triage only through severity,
  `since`, `soil_water`, `fault` and `sensor`. Raw values in the triage
  would invite the SLM to reason about them, which is the code’s job.

Some rules need more than sensor data. Readable locations need a map
from each node to its place on the farm. Groups need the irrigation
layout of each farm. `soil_water` needs no labels, because the soil
sensors show whether water arrives: the [batch 2
diagnosis](https://fr.anckalbi.net/speaking-plants/batches/b02/diagnosis.html)
found that watering had stopped from the missing morning rise in soil
moisture. Faults need no labels either: `fault` records what the data
shows, and never a cause no sensor watches, such as an empty battery or
a lost radio link. The node map and the irrigation layout are the main
open questions for the design of the ML side.

## Domain expert annotators

Synthetic data and a teacher model are a start. Domain knowledge enters
through experts, who:

- audit the dimensions and tuples, and say which cases are missing or
  unrealistic,
- review and edit synthetic messages: an edited message becomes better
  training data, and the difference from the draft shows where the
  teacher’s judgement is weak,
- do error analysis on model outputs, by writing a free-text note on
  what is wrong (open coding) and then grouping the notes into failure
  modes (axial coding),
- label outputs as pass or fail for each failure mode, to align the
  judges described under Evaluation,
- write messages for real cases, in the same format.

Experts start from drafts rather than blank pages, which is faster and
gives more consistent messages. For the first task, they must read and
write Brazilian Portuguese.

The dataset of expert-reviewed examples is the lasting artifact, not the
model. Each model is rebuilt from a version of the dataset, so it is
always possible to say whose expertise, from which version of the data,
went into which model.

A minimal annotation app, built with FastHTML and storing its data in
SQLite, supports this work. It shows one triage input next to its
message. The expert can edit the message, mark it as pass or fail, and
write a note.

## Evaluation

Evaluation decides whether a model is good enough, and so which board it
needs. Three rules hold throughout:

- every model, including the untuned base model, is scored on the same
  held-out test set,
- once expert-reviewed examples exist, the test set is weighted towards
  them, because synthetic data can train a model but should not be its
  final judge,
- final scores are measured on the target board.

### Checks computed by code

Some failure modes can be checked by comparing a message with its triage
input, without any labels:

- **Format:** every paragraph starts with a marker and a location,
  followed by a colon.
- **Coverage:** every item in the input has its paragraph.
- **No invented items:** every paragraph names a location from the
  input, and no location has two paragraphs.
- **Severity:** each paragraph has the marker of its item’s severity,
  👀, ⚠️ or 🚨.
- **No numbers:** the message contains no digits outside its locations,
  so no readings, counts or dates. Numbers that are part of a location,
  such as row 3, are allowed.
- **Length:** the message is at most 600 characters long.
- **Amount:** each cluster or widespread item uses its record’s
  [`amount`](https://franckalbinet.github.io/edgeslm/coffee.html#amount)
  word.

### Judges for the other failure modes

Other failure modes need judgement, such as whether the action fits what
the triage reports. They follow the method of [LLM as a
judge](https://fr.anckalbi.net/posts/llm-as-a-judge/):

1.  Error analysis by experts finds the failure modes.
2.  Each failure mode gets its own judge, a large model that labels a
    message as pass or fail for that one failure mode.
3.  Expert labels are split into a training set (10 to 20%, for few-shot
    examples in the judge’s prompt), a development set (40 to 45%, to
    refine the prompt) and a test set (40 to 45%). No example moves
    between sets.
4.  On the test set, the judge’s true positive rate (TPR, the share of
    good messages it passes) and true negative rate (TNR, the share of
    bad messages it fails) are measured against the expert labels.
5.  The judge’s observed pass rate on new messages is corrected with the
    Rogan-Gladen formula, which needs TPR + TNR \> 1:

$$\theta = \frac{\text{observed rate} + \text{TNR} - 1}{\text{TPR} + \text{TNR} - 1}$$

6.  A bootstrap over the test set gives a 95% confidence interval for
    the corrected rate.

## Proof of concept

The proof of concept is for a meeting, and has four aims:

1.  Explain the setup and why: the use case, and the problem it
    addresses.
2.  Show that an SLM can be fine-tuned for the task, and how much data
    it needs.
3.  Explain the role of domain experts: auditing and improving synthetic
    data, annotating new data, and error analysis for the judges.
4.  Show why AI at the edge suits this task: hosted LLM inference costs
    money and energy, farm data is sensitive, and the task needs only a
    small part of a large model’s expertise.

It uses synthetic data only, in English. The expert phase is explained
rather than run, and the annotation app shows how it would work. The
steps:

1.  **Schema and sampler:** the triage JSON schema, the 27 tuples, and
    random variation within each.
2.  **Teacher messages:** Claude Haiku writes the message for each
    sampled input, as described under Choice of teacher, and a sample is
    checked by hand.
3.  **Baseline:** candidate base models of about 2B parameters or
    smaller, so that they run on the UNO Q, are scored on the 270 test
    inputs.
4.  **Metric:** the checks computed by code. A breakdown by tuple is not
    done yet.
5.  **Fine-tuning:** LoRA with MLX on Apple Silicon, trained on 50, 100
    and 199 examples, where 199 is every Haiku message in the training
    set that passes the checks. The scores against the number of
    examples form a learning curve, which answers how much data the task
    needs. With 100 examples, both models pass every check in 255 or
    more of the 270 test messages, so the proof of concept does not
    train on larger sets.
6.  **Export and edge demo:** the best model is converted to GGUF, run
    with llama.cpp, and handed to a colleague with an Arduino UNO Q,
    with example inputs, the prompt and the command, to measure speed
    and memory on the board.
7.  **Annotation app:** the minimal FastHTML app, shown on a few
    synthetic examples.
8.  **Presentation**, built from the results of steps 3 to 7.

## After the proof of concept

The proof of concept makes one pass through the pipeline on synthetic
data. The project then repeats the pipeline in rounds, on two tracks
that run side by side: the triage track builds the input, and the
message track builds the model that writes the message. The triage
contract is the only interface between them.

### The triage track

The domain project keeps collecting sensor data on the farms and
develops the triage: the features, the ML model, and the node map and
irrigation layout listed as open questions under Triage contract. Until
the real triage is ready, the generator in
[`01_coffee`](../01_coffee.ipynb) stands in for it. When it is ready,
its records join the generated ones, first as test inputs and then as
training inputs. A change to the contract, such as a new field or a new
kind of fault, starts a new round on the message track.

### The message track

Each round on the message track has these steps:

1.  **Inputs:** synthetic triage records, and real ones as the triage
    produces them. Experts audit the dimensions and tuples and name the
    missing cases.
2.  **Messages:** the teacher drafts a message for each input. Experts
    review and edit a sample in the annotation app, and their edited
    messages replace the drafts in the training set.
3.  **Fine-tuning:** the small model is trained on the current version
    of the dataset.
4.  **Evaluation:** the code checks run on every message. Experts
    annotate a sample of the small model’s messages, first with
    free-text notes and then with a pass or fail for each failure mode,
    as described under Domain expert annotators. Once there are enough
    expert labels, an LLM judge for each failure mode, aligned on those
    labels, scores the failure modes that code cannot check.
5.  **Deployment:** the model is exported to GGUF, scored again on the
    board, and installed on the gateways.
6.  **Field review:** experts review a sample of the messages written on
    real farms, and those cases enter the next round.

Each round ends with a new version of the dataset and the model built
from it. Failure modes found in error analysis become new code checks or
judges, and missing cases become new tuples.

## Terms

- **SLM:** small language model, here with up to about 4 billion
  parameters.
- **LoRA:** Low-Rank Adaptation, a fine-tuning method that trains small
  adapter matrices next to the frozen weights of a model. Not to be
  confused with **LoRa**, the long-range radio that links the nodes to
  the gateway. In code, we avoid a bare `lora` name.
- **GGUF:** the single-file model format of llama.cpp, holding the
  weights, usually quantized, with the tokenizer and metadata.
- **Node:** a sensor station on one plant, which stands for the plants
  around it. Only some plants carry one.
- **Triage:** the output of the domain code, listing the nodes to watch
  or fix for one farm and one day.
- **Tuple:** one combination of levels, one from each dimension.
- **Teacher:** the large model that writes reference messages.
- **Failure mode:** one specific way a message can be wrong, found by
  error analysis.
